title: PHY_102 — End of Semester Objective Exam

questions.q: A metal sphere is left with a net charge of +3.2 × 10⁻⁹ C. Take e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. How many electrons were removed from it?
questions.concept: Counting electrons with q = ne
questions.why:
Charge is quantised, q = ne, so n = |q|/e = 3.2 × 10⁻⁹ / 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹. The mantissas give 3.2/1.6 = 2.0 and the powers give 10⁻⁹⁻⁽⁻¹⁹⁾ = 10¹⁰, so n = 2.0 × 10¹⁰ electrons. The sphere is positive, so those electrons were removed.

5.0 × 10⁻¹¹ divides the wrong way round (e/q); 5.1 × 10⁻²⁸ multiplies q by e instead of dividing; 2.0 × 10¹¹ is a power-of-ten slip in subtracting the exponents.

questions.q: Identical metal spheres P, Q and R stand on insulating stands. P carries +12 nC, Q is neutral and R carries −4.0 nC. P is touched to Q and separated, then P is touched to R and separated. What charge does P carry at the end?
questions.concept: Charge sharing through successive contacts
questions.why:
Identical conductors in contact share the total equally. First contact: P and Q each get (+12 + 0)/2 = +6.0 nC. Second contact: P and R each get (+6.0 + (−4.0))/2 = +1.0 nC. So P ends with +1.0 nC.

+6.0 nC stops after the first contact; +4.0 nC averages +12 and −4 and forgets that Q took half of P's charge first; +2.7 nC shares the total +8 nC between all three spheres at once, which never happens because they touch in pairs.

questions.q: Point charges of −5.0 μC and −2.0 μC are held 6.0 cm apart in vacuum. Take k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². What is the force between them?
questions.concept: Coulomb's law with two charges
questions.why:
Convert first: r = 0.060 m, so r² = 3.6 × 10⁻³ m². F = k|q₁q₂|/r² = (9.0 × 10⁹)(5.0 × 10⁻⁶)(2.0 × 10⁻⁶)/(3.6 × 10⁻³) = 9.0 × 10⁻²/3.6 × 10⁻³ = 25 N. Both charges are negative, so the force is repulsive.

1.5 N divides by r instead of r²; 2.5 × 10⁻³ N leaves r in centimetres, which costs a factor of 10⁴; the attractive option treats two like charges as unlike.

questions.q: A point charge Q = −8.0 nC is fixed in vacuum. Take k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². What is the electric field at a point 3.0 cm from Q?
questions.concept: Field of a point charge
questions.why:
E = k|Q|/r² with r = 0.030 m, r² = 9.0 × 10⁻⁴ m²: E = (9.0 × 10⁹)(8.0 × 10⁻⁹)/(9.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 72/9.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 8.0 × 10⁴ N/C. The source is negative, so the field points toward it.

2.4 × 10³ N/C forgets to square r; 8.0 N/C leaves r in centimetres; the 'away from Q' option has the right size but the direction of a negative charge's field wrong.

questions.q: A small sphere of mass 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ kg hangs at rest in a uniform electric field of 5.0 × 10⁴ N/C directed vertically upward. Take g = 9.8 m/s². What charge does the sphere carry?
questions.concept: Charge in equilibrium under gravity and a field
questions.why:
At rest the electric force balances the weight: qE = mg, so q = mg/E = (2.0 × 10⁻⁶)(9.8)/(5.0 × 10⁴) = 1.96 × 10⁻⁵/5.0 × 10⁴ = 3.9 × 10⁻¹⁰ C. The field is upward and the force must be upward, so the charge is positive. Accept 3.9 to 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ C.

The negative option would be pushed downward by an upward field; 4.0 × 10⁻¹¹ C leaves out g; 9.8 × 10⁻¹ C multiplies by E instead of dividing.

questions.q: Two point charges of +6.0 nC each are fixed on the x-axis at x = 0 and x = 0.30 m. Take k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². What is the resultant electric field at x = 0.15 m?
questions.concept: Cancellation of fields from equal charges
questions.why:
Each charge is 0.15 m from the point, and each contributes k(6.0 × 10⁻⁹)/(0.15)² = 54/2.25 × 10⁻² = 2.4 × 10³ N/C. The left charge pushes in the +x direction and the right charge pushes in the −x direction, equal sizes in opposite directions, so the resultant is zero.

2.4 × 10³ N/C is one contribution alone; 4.8 × 10³ N/C adds the two magnitudes as if they pointed the same way; 6.0 × 10² N/C uses the full 0.30 m separation instead of the 0.15 m to the field point.

questions.q: Two point charges attract each other with a force F when their centres are 4.0 cm apart. At what separation is the force between them F/9?
questions.concept: Inverse-square dependence of the Coulomb force
questions.why:
F ∝ 1/r², so dividing the force by 9 means multiplying r² by 9, that is multiplying r by √9 = 3. The new separation is 3 × 4.0 = 12 cm.

36 cm multiplies the distance by 9 instead of by its square root; 1.3 cm and 0.44 cm move the charges closer, which increases the force rather than reducing it.

questions.q: Take e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Which of these measured net charges is impossible for an isolated object?
questions.concept: Quantisation of charge
questions.why:
Charge is quantised: every net charge is a whole-number multiple of e. Divide each by 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹: 3.2/1.6 = 2, 8.0/1.6 = 5, 16/1.6 = 10, but 4.0/1.6 = 2.5, which is not a whole number. So −4.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ C cannot exist as a net charge.

The other three are 2e, 5e and 10e in size, all permitted. Note that this is quantisation, not conservation: conservation limits how a total may change, quantisation limits which values it may take.

questions.q: Charges of +2.0 nC are fixed on the x-axis at x = 0 and at x = 0.30 m. A +1.0 nC charge is placed at x = 0.10 m. Take k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². What is the net force on it?
questions.concept: Net force from two collinear charges
questions.why:
From the charge at x = 0, distance 0.10 m: F₁ = (9.0 × 10⁹)(2.0 × 10⁻⁹)(1.0 × 10⁻⁹)/(0.10)² = 1.8 × 10⁻⁸/1.0 × 10⁻² = 1.8 × 10⁻⁶ N, repulsive, so +x. From the charge at x = 0.30 m, distance 0.20 m: F₂ = 1.8 × 10⁻⁸/4.0 × 10⁻² = 4.5 × 10⁻⁷ N, repulsive, so −x. The arrows oppose, so subtract: 1.8 × 10⁻⁶ − 4.5 × 10⁻⁷ = 1.35 × 10⁻⁶ N in the +x direction, toward the further charge.

2.25 × 10⁻⁶ N adds two arrows that point opposite ways; the −x option keeps the size but sends it toward the nearer charge; 1.8 × 10⁻⁶ N ignores the second charge entirely.

questions.q: A +2.0 nC charge sits at x = 0 and a −8.0 nC charge at x = 0.60 m. Take k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². What is the electric field at x = 0.20 m?
questions.concept: Superposition of fields on a line
questions.why:
Distances from the field point are 0.20 m and 0.40 m. E₁ = (9.0 × 10⁹)(2.0 × 10⁻⁹)/(0.20)² = 18/4.0 × 10⁻² = 450 N/C, pointing away from the positive charge, so +x. E₂ = (9.0 × 10⁹)(8.0 × 10⁻⁹)/(0.40)² = 72/0.16 = 450 N/C, pointing toward the negative charge, so also +x. Same direction, so add: 900 N/C in the +x direction.

Zero subtracts two fields that in fact agree in direction; the −x option reverses both arrows; 650 N/C uses 0.60 m rather than the 0.40 m from the second charge to the field point.

questions.q: Two point charges of equal magnitude q, one positive and one negative, are fixed 0.20 m apart. The electric field at the midpoint of the line joining them has magnitude 3.6 × 10⁴ N/C. Take k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². What is q?
questions.concept: Finding a charge from a superposed field
questions.why:
At the midpoint each charge is 0.10 m away, and both fields point from the positive charge toward the negative one, so the magnitudes add: E = 2kq/r² . Rearranging, q = Er²/(2k) = (3.6 × 10⁴)(1.0 × 10⁻²)/(1.8 × 10¹⁰) = 360/1.8 × 10¹⁰ = 2.0 × 10⁻⁸ C, that is 20 nC.

4.0 × 10⁻⁸ C forgets that two charges contribute; 8.0 × 10⁻⁸ C uses the full 0.20 m instead of the 0.10 m to the midpoint; 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ C is a power-of-ten slip.

questions.q: In a region the electric field lines are straight, parallel and evenly spaced, all pointing due west. An electron is released from rest in this region. How does it move?
options: It remains at rest, because evenly spaced lines mean no net force
questions.concept: Motion of a charge in a uniform field
questions.why:
Field lines show the direction of the force on a positive charge, so an electron, being negative, feels a force opposite to the lines: due east. Evenly spaced parallel lines mean the field is uniform, so the force F = qE is constant and the acceleration is constant, not the speed.

Due west follows the lines and ignores the electron's sign; constant speed would need zero net force; the last option confuses uniform spacing with zero field.

questions.q: At a point the electric field is 2.5 × 10⁴ N/C directed due east. Take e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What force acts on an electron placed at that point?
questions.concept: Force on a charge in a field, F = qE
questions.why:
F = |q|E = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)(2.5 × 10⁴) = 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ N. The electron is negative, so the force is antiparallel to E: due west.

The 'due east' option forgets the sign reversal; 6.3 × 10²² N divides E by e instead of multiplying; 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ N is a power-of-ten slip in adding the exponents.

questions.q: Charges are fixed on the x-axis: −4.0 μC at x = 0, +3.0 μC at x = 0.30 m and +6.0 μC at x = 0.60 m. Take k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². What is the net force on the +3.0 μC charge?
questions.concept: Net force from two collinear charges
questions.why:
Both neighbours are 0.30 m away, so r² = 9.0 × 10⁻² m² each time. From the −4.0 μC on the left: F₁ = (9.0 × 10⁹)(4.0 × 10⁻⁶)(3.0 × 10⁻⁶)/(9.0 × 10⁻²) = 0.108/0.09 = 1.2 N, attractive, so −x. From the +6.0 μC on the right: F₂ = 0.162/0.09 = 1.8 N, repulsive, so also −x. The arrows agree, so add: 3.0 N in the −x direction.

0.60 N subtracts them as if they opposed; 1.8 N leaves out the −4.0 μC charge; the +x option gets both directions backwards.

questions.q: Charges A and B both exert electric forces on a third charge C. A fourth charge D is now brought close to C. What happens to the force that A alone exerts on C?
options: Reduced, because D shields C from A
Reversed in direction if D is negative
questions.concept: Superposition of electric forces
questions.why:
By the principle of superposition the total force on C is the vector sum of the separate pairwise forces, and each pairwise force is given by Coulomb's law for that pair alone. Nothing in kq_Aq_C/r² refers to any other charge, so the force from A on C is unchanged; what changes is the total, which now has D's contribution added in.

Shielding is not an electrostatic effect between point charges; doubling or reversing would require A's charge or its distance to change, and neither does.

questions.q: A +9.0 nC charge is at x = 0 and a +4.0 nC charge at x = 0.50 m. At which point between them is the resultant electric field zero?
questions.concept: Locating the point where two fields cancel
questions.why:
Between two positive charges the two fields point in opposite directions, so they cancel where the magnitudes match: k(9.0)/x² = k(4.0)/(0.50 − x)² in nanocoulombs. Take square roots: (0.50 − x)/x = √(4/9) = 2/3, so 1.5(0.50 − x) = x, 0.75 = 2.5x, x = 0.30 m from the +9.0 nC charge.

0.35 m uses the ratio 9:4 without taking the square root; 0.25 m is the midpoint, which would only be right for equal charges; 0.20 m puts the null nearer the larger charge, which cannot happen.

questions.q: A cell of emf 12 V and internal resistance 1.5 Ω is connected across a 4.5 Ω resistor. What current flows?
questions.concept: Current in a single loop with internal resistance
questions.why:
Round the loop the emf drives current through both resistances: ε = I(R + r), so I = ε/(R + r) = 12/(4.5 + 1.5) = 12/6.0 = 2.0 A.

2.7 A leaves the internal resistance out (12/4.5); 8.0 A divides by r alone; 4.0 A subtracts r from R instead of adding it.

questions.q: The terminal p.d. V of a cell is measured at several currents I, and the points lie on a straight line through (0.50 A, 5.70 V) and (2.00 A, 5.10 V). What are the emf and the internal resistance of the cell?
questions.concept: Getting emf and internal resistance from a V-I line
questions.why:
The line is V = ε − rI. Gradient = (5.10 − 5.70)/(2.00 − 0.50) = −0.60/1.50 = −0.40 V/A, so r = 0.40 Ω. Then ε = V + Ir = 5.70 + (0.50)(0.40) = 5.90 V, which is the value extrapolated back to I = 0.

5.70 V takes a measured terminal p.d. as the emf; 2.5 Ω uses the negative reciprocal of the gradient, which has the wrong units; 5.50 V subtracts Ir where it should be added, because V is already the reduced value.

questions.q: A straight rod 0.25 m long moves at 8.0 m/s perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.60 T, the field being perpendicular to the rod. What emf is induced between its ends?
questions.concept: Motional emf, e = Bvl
questions.why:
The rod sweeps out area at a rate lv, so the flux linked changes at Blv and ε = Bvl = (0.60)(8.0)(0.25) = 1.2 V.

0.15 V leaves out the speed; 4.8 V leaves out the length; 2.0 V leaves out the flux density. Checking units settles it: T × m/s × m = V.

questions.q: A coil of 250 turns has area 4.0 × 10⁻³ m² with its plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field. The field rises steadily from 0.20 T to 0.60 T in 0.50 s. What is the magnitude of the induced emf?
questions.concept: Faraday's law with N turns
questions.why:
Φ = BA, so ΔΦ = AΔB = (4.0 × 10⁻³)(0.60 − 0.20) = 1.6 × 10⁻³ Wb per turn. Then |ε| = N ΔΦ/Δt = 250 × 1.6 × 10⁻³/0.50 = 0.80 V. The minus sign in Faraday's law gives direction only, so it is dropped for a magnitude.

1.2 V uses the final field 0.60 T instead of the change; 0.40 V forgets to divide by the time; 3.2 × 10⁻³ V leaves out the 250 turns.

questions.q: A 25 μF capacitor is charged to a potential difference of 400 V. How much energy does it store?
questions.concept: Energy stored in a capacitor
questions.why:
U = ½CV² = ½(25 × 10⁻⁶)(400)² = ½(25 × 10⁻⁶)(1.6 × 10⁵) = 2.0 J.

4.0 J forgets the factor ½, which is there because the p.d. rises from 0 to V as the charge is added; 5.0 × 10⁻³ J uses V instead of V²; 1.0 × 10⁻² J is the charge Q = CV in coulombs, not an energy.

questions.q: In vacuum the electric field in a region has magnitude 5.0 × 10⁵ V/m. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m. What is the energy stored per unit volume?
questions.concept: Energy density of an electric field
questions.why:
u = ½ε₀E² = ½(8.85 × 10⁻¹²)(5.0 × 10⁵)² = ½(8.85 × 10⁻¹²)(2.5 × 10¹¹) = 1.1 J/m³, accepting 1.10 to 1.11.

2.2 J/m³ omits the ½; 2.2 × 10⁻⁶ J/m³ uses E instead of E²; 4.4 × 10⁻⁶ J/m³ makes both slips at once. The unit J/m³ marks this as a density: multiply by the volume to get joules.

questions.q: A parallel-plate capacitor in vacuum has plates of area 0.020 m² separated by 2.0 mm, and is connected across a 300 V supply. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m. How much energy is stored?
questions.concept: Capacitance and energy of parallel plates
questions.why:
First the capacitance: C = ε₀A/d = (8.85 × 10⁻¹²)(0.020)/(2.0 × 10⁻³) = 8.85 × 10⁻¹¹ F. Then U = ½CV² = ½(8.85 × 10⁻¹¹)(9.0 × 10⁴) = 3.98 × 10⁻⁶ J, so 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ J, accepting 3.9 to 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ J.

8.0 × 10⁻⁶ J forgets the ½; 1.3 × 10⁻⁸ J uses V instead of V²; 4.0 × 10⁻⁹ J leaves the separation in millimetres, making C a thousand times too small.

questions.q: A solid copper block is placed in a steady external electric field and left to reach electrostatic equilibrium. What is the electric field deep inside the metal?
options: The external field divided by the dielectric constant of copper
Equal in size to the external field but reversed in direction
questions.concept: Field inside a conductor in equilibrium
questions.why:
A conductor has free electrons. They keep moving until the field they create inside exactly cancels the applied field, and once the interior field is zero there is nothing left to drive them, which is what equilibrium means. So E = 0 inside the metal.

'Divided by the dielectric constant' is what happens inside an insulator, whose bound charges only reduce the field; the field is not simply passed through unchanged, and a reversed field of equal size would keep pushing charge the other way and could not be a resting state.

questions.q: A battery of emf 9.0 V and internal resistance 0.60 Ω supplies a current of 1.5 A. What are its terminal p.d. and the power dissipated inside the battery?
questions.concept: Terminal p.d. and power lost inside a source
questions.why:
On discharge V = ε − Ir = 9.0 − (1.5)(0.60) = 9.0 − 0.90 = 8.1 V. The power wasted inside is P = I²r = (1.5)²(0.60) = 1.35 W.

9.9 V adds the lost volts instead of subtracting them, which is the charging case; 0.90 W quotes the lost volts as if they were a power; 12.2 W is VI, the power delivered to the external circuit, not the power lost inside.

questions.q: Charges of +5.0 nC and −5.0 nC are held 4.0 mm apart. What is the magnitude of the electric dipole moment of the pair?
questions.concept: Electric dipole moment p = qd
questions.why:
p = qd uses the magnitude of either charge, not the sum: p = (5.0 × 10⁻⁹)(4.0 × 10⁻³) = 2.0 × 10⁻¹¹ C·m, directed from the negative charge toward the positive one.

4.0 × 10⁻¹¹ C·m adds the two charges first, but the pair is neutral overall so that sum is meaningless; 2.0 × 10⁻⁸ C·m leaves the separation in millimetres; 1.3 × 10⁻⁶ C·m divides q by d instead of multiplying.

questions.q: A dipole of moment 6.0 × 10⁻¹² C·m is placed in a uniform electric field with its axis at 30° to the field, and feels a torque of 9.0 × 10⁻⁷ N·m. What is the field strength?
questions.concept: Torque on a dipole in a uniform field
questions.why:
τ = pE sin θ, so E = τ/(p sin θ) = 9.0 × 10⁻⁷/[(6.0 × 10⁻¹²)(sin 30°)] = 9.0 × 10⁻⁷/(3.0 × 10⁻¹²) = 3.0 × 10⁵ N/C.

1.5 × 10⁵ N/C leaves out sin θ; 7.5 × 10⁴ N/C multiplies by sin 30° instead of dividing; 1.7 × 10⁵ N/C uses cos 30° in place of sin 30°.

questions.q: A dipole of moment 2.5 × 10⁻¹² C·m sits in a uniform field of 4.0 × 10⁵ N/C, aligned with the field. How much work must be done on it to turn its axis until it is perpendicular to the field?
questions.concept: Potential energy of a dipole in a field
questions.why:
U = −pE cos θ. Aligned: U₀ = −pE = −(2.5 × 10⁻¹²)(4.0 × 10⁵) = −1.0 × 10⁻⁶ J. Perpendicular: U₉₀ = 0. The work needed is the increase in energy, W = U₉₀ − U₀ = +1.0 × 10⁻⁶ J.

The negative value is ΔU with the subtraction the wrong way round; 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ J is the work to turn all the way to 180°; zero would mean the two orientations were equally stable, but the aligned position is the stable one.

questions.q: A point lies on the perpendicular bisector of a short dipole, at a distance much larger than the charge separation. Which statement describes the potential and the field there?
options: V = 0, and E is antiparallel to p
V is a maximum, and E = 0
V = 0, and E is parallel to p
questions.concept: Dipole potential and field on the equatorial plane
questions.why:
V = kp cos θ/r², and on the bisector θ = 90°, so cos θ = 0 and V = 0 everywhere on that plane. The field does not vanish: the two contributions have equal magnitudes, their components along the bisector cancel and the components parallel to the axis survive, giving E = kp/r³ directed from the positive charge toward the negative one, that is antiparallel to p.

A potential of zero on a surface does not mean the field is zero, because E measures how fast V changes across the surface, not its value; the 'parallel to p' option has that direction reversed, and the maximum of V is on the axis, not here.

questions.q: A battery of emf 12.0 V and internal resistance 0.40 Ω is being charged by an external supply that drives a current of 3.0 A into its positive terminal. What is the potential difference across its terminals?
questions.concept: Terminal voltage of a source on charge
questions.why:
On charge the driving supply must push current through the internal resistance as well as against the emf, so V = ε + Ir = 12.0 + (3.0)(0.40) = 12.0 + 1.2 = 13.2 V.

10.8 V uses the discharge formula V = ε − Ir; 12.0 V ignores the internal resistance, which is only right at zero current; 1.2 V is the Ir term alone.

questions.q: A 10 V source through a 5.0 Ω resistor and a 20 V source through a 10 Ω resistor both feed node A, and A returns to ground through a 10 Ω resistor. Both sources have their negative terminals grounded and have negligible internal resistance. What is the voltage at A?
questions.concept: Nodal analysis at a single node
questions.why:
Take ground as the reference and apply the junction rule at A, writing each branch current as (far-end voltage − V_A)/R: (10 − V)/5 + (20 − V)/10 = V/10. Multiply by 10: 2(10 − V) + (20 − V) = V, so 40 − 3V = V, giving V = 10 V. As a check, the branch currents are 0 A, 1.0 A and 1.0 A, which balance.

13.3 V leaves out the 10 Ω path to ground; 15 V is the plain average of the two source voltages, which ignores the resistors; 30 V adds the sources as if they were in series.

questions.q: A 24 V source of negligible internal resistance is in series with an 8.0 Ω resistor, a 4.0 Ω resistor runs from the far end of the 8.0 Ω resistor to ground, and the output terminals are taken across the 4.0 Ω resistor. What are the Thevenin voltage and Thevenin resistance at those terminals?
questions.concept: Thevenin equivalent of a divider
questions.why:
With nothing connected across the terminals the two resistors form a divider, so V_Th = V_oc = 24 × 4.0/(8.0 + 4.0) = 8.0 V. For R_Th, zero the source, which turns the ideal voltage source into a wire, leaving 8.0 Ω in parallel with 4.0 Ω: R_Th = (8 × 4)/12 = 2.7 Ω, accepting 2.67 Ω.

12 Ω adds the resistors in series, which is what the source sees, not what the terminals see; 24 V ignores the divider; 16 V uses the wrong resistor on top of the divider fraction.

questions.q: In a superposition analysis of a linear circuit, one of the independent sources is an ideal current source that is not acting. What must replace it in the diagram?
options: A resistor equal to its internal resistance
An ideal voltage source of the same numerical value
questions.concept: Zeroing sources for superposition
questions.why:
Zeroing a source means forcing the quantity it fixes to zero. A dead current source passes zero amperes at any voltage, and the element that does that is a break in the circuit, so it becomes an open circuit. A dead voltage source holds zero volts at any current, so that one becomes a wire, a short circuit.

Swapping the two is the commonest superposition error; an ideal current source has infinite internal resistance, so replacing it by a finite resistor is wrong; replacing it by a voltage source leaves it acting.

questions.q: A 40 pF air capacitor is connected to a 50 V battery. With the battery still connected, a slab of dielectric constant κ = 4.0 is slid in to fill the gap. What are the new charge and the new stored energy?
questions.concept: Dielectric inserted at constant voltage
questions.why:
The battery stays connected, so V is held at 50 V while the capacitance rises: C = κC₀ = 4.0 × 40 pF = 160 pF. Then Q = CV = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁰)(50) = 8.0 × 10⁻⁹ C = 8.0 nC, and U = ½CV² = ½(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁰)(2500) = 2.0 × 10⁻⁷ J. The battery supplies the extra charge, so both Q and U rise by the factor κ.

2.0 nC and 5.0 × 10⁻⁸ J are the values before insertion; the mixed option keeps the old energy with the new charge; 0.50 nC and 1.3 × 10⁻⁸ J divide by κ, which is the disconnected case where Q is fixed and V falls.

questions.q: Resistors of 4.0 Ω, 6.0 Ω and 12 Ω are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance?
questions.concept: Resistors in parallel
questions.why:
1/R_eq = 1/4 + 1/6 + 1/12. Over the common denominator 12 that is 3/12 + 2/12 + 1/12 = 6/12 = 0.50 per ohm, so R_eq = 1/0.50 = 2.0 Ω. Check it against the rule that a parallel equivalent is always below the smallest branch: 2.0 Ω < 4.0 Ω.

0.50 Ω is 1/R_eq left uninverted; 22 Ω adds them as if in series; 7.3 Ω is their average, which is not how either combination works.

questions.q: A 6.0 Ω resistor is in series with two 8.0 Ω resistors that are in parallel with each other, and the whole combination is across a 20 V battery of negligible internal resistance. What current does the battery supply?
questions.concept: Series and parallel combination in a circuit
questions.why:
Two equal resistors in parallel give half of one: 8.0/2 = 4.0 Ω. That sits in series with the 6.0 Ω, so R_eq = 6.0 + 4.0 = 10 Ω, and I = V/R_eq = 20/10 = 2.0 A.

0.91 A adds all three in series (22 Ω); 1.4 A uses only one of the parallel pair (14 Ω); 5.0 A uses the parallel pair alone and forgets the 6.0 Ω in series.

questions.q: Five wires meet at a junction. Currents of 4.0 A and 2.5 A flow into it, and currents of 3.0 A and 1.5 A flow out along two of the others. What is the current in the fifth wire?
questions.concept: Kirchhoff's junction rule
questions.why:
Charge cannot pile up at a junction, so the current in equals the current out. In: 4.0 + 2.5 = 6.5 A. Out so far: 3.0 + 1.5 = 4.5 A. The fifth wire must carry the remaining 6.5 − 4.5 = 2.0 A out of the junction.

'Into the junction' would make the total in 8.5 A against 4.5 A out; 11 A adds every current in the problem; 1.0 A comes from subtracting the two outgoing currents from each other.

questions.q: A single loop contains a 20 V battery of internal resistance 1.0 Ω and an 8.0 V battery of internal resistance 0.50 Ω connected so that they oppose each other, together with external resistors of 4.5 Ω and 2.0 Ω. What current flows?
questions.concept: Loop rule with two opposing emfs
questions.why:
Walking round the loop with the assumed current, the emfs enter with opposite signs because the batteries face each other, so only their difference drives the current: 20 − 8.0 = 12 V. Every resistance in the loop counts, internal ones included: 1.0 + 0.50 + 4.5 + 2.0 = 8.0 Ω. Then 12 = I(8.0), so I = 1.5 A.

3.5 A adds the emfs, which would be right only if both drove the current the same way; 1.8 A leaves out the two internal resistances; 2.5 A uses the 20 V battery alone.

questions.q: Travelling round a loop you pass through a resistor in the direction opposite to the assumed current, and then through a battery, entering at its + terminal and leaving at its − terminal. What signs do these two terms carry in the loop equation?
questions.concept: Sign rules for the loop equation
questions.why:
Walking against the assumed current through a resistor means walking from the low-potential end to the high-potential end, a rise, so the term is +IR. Crossing a source from + to − is a fall in potential, so the emf enters as −ε.

The emf sign depends only on the order in which the terminals are crossed, never on which way the current runs, and the IR sign depends only on the travel direction relative to the current arrow. Reversing the direction of travel would flip both signs together and leave the solution unchanged.

questions.q: In a bridge circuit the assumed current I₁ = 4.0 A arrives at junction b, while the assumed currents I₃ (from b to d) and I₅ (from b to c) leave it. Solving the network gives I₅ = −1.5 A. What is I₃?
questions.concept: Junction rule with a negative branch current
questions.why:
The junction rule at b reads I₁ = I₃ + I₅. Substituting the signed value, 4.0 = I₃ + (−1.5), so I₃ = 4.0 + 1.5 = 5.5 A, in the assumed direction from b to d. The negative I₅ simply means 1.5 A actually flows from c to b, so it arrives at b along with I₁ and the arm b to d has to carry both.

2.5 A treats I₅ as 1.5 A leaving b, ignoring its sign; −5.5 A carries the minus sign into the wrong branch; 1.5 A confuses the two arms.

questions.q: A 12 V battery of negligible internal resistance is connected across a 6.0 Ω resistor and a 12 Ω resistor joined in parallel. What total power does the battery deliver?
questions.concept: Power in parallel branches
questions.why:
In parallel each resistor has the full 12 V across it, so P = V²/R branch by branch: 144/6.0 = 24 W and 144/12 = 12 W, giving 36 W in total. The same follows from R_eq = 4.0 Ω and P = V²/R_eq = 144/4.0 = 36 W.

8.0 W treats the resistors as being in series (18 Ω); 24 W and 12 W are the two branches taken singly, and the smaller resistance is the one taking the larger share.

questions.q: Walking from point a to point b you pass through a 5.0 Ω resistor against the direction of its 1.2 A current, then through a 6.0 V battery from its + terminal to its − terminal, then through a 2.0 Ω resistor in the direction of the same 1.2 A current. What is V_b − V_a?
questions.concept: Potential difference along a path
questions.why:
Add the potential changes in order. Against the current through 5.0 Ω is a rise: +(1.2)(5.0) = +6.0 V. Crossing the battery from + to − is a fall: −6.0 V. With the current through 2.0 Ω is a fall: −(1.2)(2.0) = −2.4 V. Total: 6.0 − 6.0 − 2.4 = −2.4 V, so b sits 2.4 V below a.

+2.4 V has every sign reversed, which is what you get by walking from b to a; −14.4 V makes both IR terms negative by using the travel direction alone; +9.6 V crosses the battery with the wrong sign.

questions.q: An alternating supply has an rms voltage of 110 V. What is its peak voltage?
questions.concept: Converting between rms and peak values
questions.why:
V_rms = V_max/√2, so V_max = √2 V_rms = 1.4142 × 110 = 155.6 V, that is about 156 V. Accept 155 to 156 V. The peak of a sinusoid is always larger than its rms value, which is the quick check on the direction of the conversion.

77.8 V multiplies by 0.7071 instead of dividing, giving a peak smaller than the rms value; 220 V doubles; 110 V confuses the two values.

questions.q: An alternating supply has a period of 20 ms. What are its frequency and its angular frequency?
questions.concept: Period, frequency and angular frequency
questions.why:
f = 1/T = 1/0.020 = 50 Hz, and ω = 2πf = 2π(50) = 314 rad/s, equivalently ω = 2π/T. Accept 314 to 315 rad/s.

'50 rad/s' uses f where ω belongs and is out by the factor 2π; 20 Hz reads the period in milliseconds as a frequency; the last option keeps the period in seconds without inverting it.

questions.q: A source v = 80 sin(120πt) V, with t in seconds, is connected across a 25 Ω resistor. What is the rms current?
questions.concept: Peak and rms current in a resistor
questions.why:
Read the amplitude off the equation: V_max = 80 V. Then I_max = V_max/R = 80/25 = 3.2 A, and I_rms = 0.7071 I_max = 2.26 A, so 2.3 A. Accept 2.2 to 2.3 A. Equally, V_rms = 56.6 V and I_rms = 56.6/25 = 2.3 A.

3.2 A is the peak current, not the rms; 4.5 A multiplies by √2 instead of dividing; 1.6 A halves the peak instead of dividing by √2.

questions.q: A 40 Ω resistor carries an alternating current i = 2.4 sin(ωt) A. What average power does it dissipate?
questions.concept: Average power from a peak current
questions.why:
The average power uses the rms current: I_rms = 2.4/√2 = 1.697 A, so P_av = I²_rms R = (1.697)²(40) = 2.88 × 40 = 115 W. Accept 115 to 116 W. The same thing in one step is P_av = ½I²_max R.

230 W uses the peak current in P = I²R and so doubles the answer; 58 W applies the factor 0.7071 twice; 96 W multiplies the peak current by 40 as if it were a voltage.

questions.q: An AC ammeter in series with a heating element reads 5.0 A. What does that reading tell you about the current?
options: A steady direct current of 5.0 A would heat the element at the same average rate
The current reaches 5.0 A at the peak of each cycle
The average of the current over one complete cycle is 5.0 A
The current has the value 5.0 A at every instant
questions.concept: Meaning of an rms value
questions.why:
AC meters are calibrated to read rms values, and the rms value is defined as the steady direct current that would dissipate the same average power in a resistive load. So 5.0 A rms and 5.0 A DC heat the element equally.

The peak is larger, 5.0 × √2 = 7.1 A; the plain average over a complete cycle is zero, since the two half-cycles cancel, which is exactly why rms values are used instead; and an alternating current is not constant at any value.

questions.q: A voltage is given by v = 150 sin(100πt) V, with t in seconds. What is the instantaneous voltage at t = 2.0 ms?
questions.concept: Instantaneous value of a sinusoidal voltage
questions.why:
The angle is ωt = 100π × 2.0 × 10⁻³ = 0.2π rad = 36°, and sin 36° = 0.588. So v = 150 × 0.588 = 88 V. Accept 88 to 89 V.

150 V is the peak, reached only when ωt = 90°; 1.6 V comes from treating the angle 0.628 as degrees rather than radians; 106 V is the rms value, which is not what an instantaneous value asks for.

questions.q: A heater is rated 1.5 kW when connected to a 250 V rms supply. What peak current does it draw?
questions.concept: Peak current from a power rating
questions.why:
A power rating uses rms values: I_rms = P/V_rms = 1500/250 = 6.0 A. The peak is larger by √2: I_max = 1.4142 × 6.0 = 8.5 A. Accept 8.4 to 8.5 A.

6.0 A is the rms current, which is what the meter would read but not the peak; 4.2 A multiplies by 0.7071 instead of dividing; 12 A doubles the rms value instead of using √2.

questions.q: An AC generator of peak voltage 60.0 V and frequency 50.0 Hz is connected to a 40.0 Ω resistor. What are the average and the maximum power dissipated in the resistor?
questions.concept: Average and maximum power in a resistor
questions.why:
V_rms = 0.7071 × 60.0 = 42.4 V, so P_av = V²_rms/R = 1800/40.0 = 45.0 W. The maximum power uses the peak voltage: P_max = V²_max/R = 3600/40.0 = 90.0 W, exactly twice the average, as it always is for a sinusoid across a resistor. The frequency is not needed anywhere, because nothing about a pure resistor depends on it.

90.0 W and 180 W use the peak voltage for the average as well; 22.5 W and 45.0 W apply the factor 0.7071 one time too many; equal powers would require a steady current.

questions.q: A 40 Ω resistor is in series with a 95.5 mH inductor across a 240 V rms, 50 Hz supply. Calculate the real power dissipated.
questions.concept: Real power in a series RL circuit
questions.why:
X_L = 2πfL = 2π(50)(0.0955) = 30.0 Ω, so Z = √(40² + 30²) = 50.0 Ω and I = 240/50.0 = 4.80 A. Only the resistance dissipates, so P = I²R = (4.80)²(40) = 922 W (accept 915 to 925 W).

1152 W is the apparent power VI, with cos φ left out; 1440 W uses V²/R with the whole supply voltage, but only 192 V sits across the resistor; 691 W uses sin φ = 0.80 and is the reactive power in var, not watts.

questions.q: A load draws 4.8 kW of real power and 3.6 kvar of reactive power. Calculate its power factor.
questions.concept: Power factor from the power triangle
questions.why:
The three powers form a right-angled triangle, S² = P² + Q², so S = √(4.8² + 3.6²) = √(23.04 + 12.96) = 6.0 kVA. Then PF = P/S = 4.8/6.0 = 0.80 (accept 0.79 to 0.81).

0.60 is Q/S, the reactive factor, not the power factor; 0.75 is Q/P, which is tan φ; 0.57 comes from adding P and Q arithmetically to get 8.4, but the two do not add that way.

questions.q: A workshop draws 5.0 kW at 250 V rms, 50 Hz, at a power factor of 0.60 lagging. Calculate the capacitance that must be connected in parallel with it to raise the power factor to unity.
questions.concept: Power factor correction with a parallel capacitor
questions.why:
S = P/PF = 5000/0.60 = 8333 VA, and sin φ = 0.80, so Q_load = S sin φ = 6667 var lagging. For unity power factor the capacitor must supply all of it, Q_C = 6667 var. Then C = Q_C/(ωV²) = 6667/[(314.16)(250²)] = 3.40 × 10⁻⁴ F = 340 μF (accept 335 to 345 μF).

255 μF puts the real power 5000 W in place of Q_C; 2130 μF uses f = 50 where ω = 2πf belongs; 424 μF uses the apparent power 8333 VA instead of the reactive power.

questions.q: A 15 Ω resistor, a 0.12 H inductor and a 30 μF capacitor are connected in series. Calculate the frequency at which the current in the circuit is a maximum.
questions.concept: Resonant frequency of a series RLC circuit
questions.why:
The current peaks at resonance, where X_L = X_C and Z falls to R. ω₀ = 1/√(LC) = 1/√[(0.12)(30 × 10⁻⁶)] = 1/√(3.6 × 10⁻⁶) = 527 rad/s, so f₀ = ω₀/2π = 527/6.283 = 83.9 Hz (accept 83 to 85 Hz). The resistance does not enter.

527 Hz quotes the angular frequency in rad/s as though it were a frequency in Hz; 13.4 Hz divides by 2π a second time; 44 200 Hz forgets the square root of LC.

questions.q: A resistor connected to a 60 Hz supply dissipates an average power of 480 W. What are the peak instantaneous power and the frequency at which the instantaneous power pulsates?
questions.concept: Peak and average power in a resistor
questions.why:
For a resistor v and i are in phase, so p = V₀I₀ sin²ωt = P(1 − cos 2ωt). That swings from 0 to 2P, giving a peak of 2 × 480 = 960 W, and it oscillates at 2f = 120 Hz because v and i reverse sign together and their product completes two cycles per supply cycle.

480 W and 60 Hz confuses the average with the peak and the ripple rate with the supply rate; 960 W and 60 Hz has the peak right but keeps the supply frequency; 240 W halves the average instead of doubling it.

questions.q: Two loads on the same 240 V rms supply each draw 5.0 A rms at a power factor of 0.70. One load is inductive and the other is capacitive. Which quantity differs between the two loads?
options: The sign of the reactive power
questions.concept: Leading and lagging at the same power factor
questions.why:
P = VI cos φ and cos φ is an even function, so cos(+45.6°) and cos(−45.6°) are the same number: both loads consume the same 840 W, draw the same 1200 VA and the same 5.0 A. What differs is Q = VI sin φ, which is positive for the inductive load (current lagging) and negative for the capacitive one (current leading). That is exactly why a power factor must always be written as leading or lagging.

Real power, apparent power and current are all fixed once V, I and cos φ are fixed, so none of them can distinguish the two.

questions.q: A series circuit has R = 30 Ω, X_L = 80 Ω and X_C = 40 Ω across a 100 V rms supply. Calculate the rms current and state whether it leads or lags the supply voltage.
questions.concept: Impedance and current in a series RLC circuit
questions.why:
The reactances are 180° apart, so they subtract: X = X_L − X_C = 80 − 40 = 40 Ω. Then Z = √(30² + 40²) = 50 Ω and I = 100/50 = 2.0 A (accept 1.9 to 2.1 A). X is positive, so the circuit is net inductive and the current lags.

0.81 A adds the reactances to get 120 Ω before combining with R; 'leading' gets the sign of the net reactance backwards, since X_L is the larger; 1.1 A squares all three of R, X_L and X_C and adds them, instead of subtracting the reactances first.

questions.q: A supply v(t) = 150 sin(314t) V drives a current i(t) = 6.0 sin(314t + 40°) A through a load, with t in seconds. Calculate the average power delivered to the load.
questions.concept: Average power from v(t) and i(t)
questions.why:
The phase angle between v and i is 40°, so P = ½V₀I₀ cos φ = ½(150)(6.0)(cos 40°) = 450 × 0.766 = 345 W (accept 340 to 350 W). Equivalently V_rms = 106 V, I_rms = 4.24 A and P = (106)(4.24)(0.766).

450 W drops cos φ and is the apparent power in VA; 689 W uses the peak values in P = VI cos φ instead of rms values, doubling the answer; 289 W uses sin 40° and gives the reactive power in var.

questions.q: A flat circular coil of 40 turns and radius 6.0 cm carries a current of 2.5 A. Calculate the magnitude of its magnetic dipole moment.
questions.concept: Magnetic dipole moment of a coil
questions.why:
A = πr² = π(0.060)² = 1.131 × 10⁻² m², so μ = NIA = (40)(2.5)(1.131 × 10⁻²) = 1.13 A·m² (accept 1.12 to 1.14 A·m²), directed along the normal to the coil.

0.0283 A·m² forgets the 40 turns; 4.52 A·m² uses 12 cm as the radius, that is the diameter, which multiplies the area by four; 1.13 × 10⁴ A·m² leaves the radius in centimetres.

questions.q: A coil of 60 turns, each of area 15 cm², carries 3.0 A. It sits in a uniform field of 0.25 T with the plane of the coil at 30° to the field. Calculate the torque on the coil.
questions.concept: Torque on a current loop in a field
questions.why:
μ = NIA = (60)(3.0)(15 × 10⁻⁴) = 0.27 A·m². The angle in τ = μB sin θ is measured from the normal, and the plane is at 30° to B, so the normal is at 60°. τ = (0.27)(0.25)(sin 60°) = 0.0675 × 0.866 = 0.0584 N·m (accept 0.057 to 0.060 N·m).

0.0338 N·m puts the 30° straight into the sine, reading the angle from the plane instead of the normal; 0.0675 N·m is the maximum torque μB, which needs the normal at 90°; 9.7 × 10⁻⁴ N·m leaves out the 60 turns.

questions.q: A magnetic dipole of moment 0.80 A·m² sits in a uniform field of 0.35 T. Calculate the work an external agent must do to turn it from 30° to 120°, both angles measured from the field direction.
questions.concept: Work done rotating a magnetic dipole
questions.why:
U = −μB cos θ, so W = U(120°) − U(30°) = μB(cos 30° − cos 120°) = (0.80)(0.35)(0.866 − (−0.500)) = 0.28 × 1.366 = 0.383 J (accept 0.375 to 0.390 J). It is positive, so energy must be supplied.

0.242 J keeps only the starting term, treating U(120°) as zero; 0.560 J is 2μB, the work for a complete flip from 0° to 180°; 0.140 J uses sines in place of cosines, which is the torque formula, not the energy one.

questions.q: A long straight wire carries a current of 12 A. Take μ₀/2π = 2 × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A. At what distance from the wire is the magnetic flux density 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ T?
questions.concept: Field of a long straight wire
questions.why:
B = μ₀I/2πr, so r = (μ₀/2π)(I/B) = (2 × 10⁻⁷)(12)/(3.0 × 10⁻⁵) = 2.4 × 10⁻⁶/3.0 × 10⁻⁵ = 0.080 m = 8.0 cm (accept 7.8 to 8.2 cm). The field is tangential, in circles round the wire.

28 cm takes a square root, treating the wire's field as an inverse-square law when it falls as 1/r; 0.80 cm is a power-of-ten slip in the division; 50 cm uses μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ where μ₀/2π belongs, leaving out the factor 2π.

questions.q: A solenoid 40 cm long has 1000 turns and carries 2.5 A. It is wound on an iron core of relative permeability 250. Take μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A. Calculate the flux density inside it.
questions.concept: Field inside a solenoid with a core
questions.why:
n = N/ℓ = 1000/0.40 = 2500 turns per metre. B = μᵣμ₀nI = (250)(4π × 10⁻⁷)(2500)(2.5) = 250 × 7.854 × 10⁻³ = 1.96 T (accept 1.93 to 1.99 T). The radius of the solenoid does not enter.

7.85 × 10⁻³ T is the air-cored value, with the factor 250 left out; 0.785 T uses N = 1000 in place of n = N/ℓ; 1.96 × 10⁻² T leaves the length in centimetres, so n comes out 100 times too small.

questions.q: A flat circular coil of 200 turns and radius 10 cm is to produce a flux density of 5.0 mT at its centre, where B = μ₀NI/2R. Take μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A. What current is needed?
questions.concept: Field at the centre of a circular coil
questions.why:
Rearranging, I = 2RB/(μ₀N) = 2(0.10)(5.0 × 10⁻³)/[(4π × 10⁻⁷)(200)] = 1.0 × 10⁻³/2.513 × 10⁻⁴ = 3.98 A (accept 3.9 to 4.1 A).

1.99 A drops the factor 2 in the numerator; 7.96 A uses 0.20 m, the diameter, in place of the radius; 398 A leaves the radius in centimetres.

questions.q: A closed surface is drawn so that it encloses the north pole of a bar magnet but not its south pole. What is the net magnetic flux through that surface?
options: Proportional to the strength of the enclosed pole
Equal to μ₀ times the enclosed pole strength
Equal to BA, where A is the area of the surface
questions.concept: Gauss's law for magnetism
questions.why:
There are no magnetic monopoles, so every line of B is a closed loop. Every line that enters the surface must leave it again, and the net flux through any closed surface is exactly zero. This holds no matter which part of the magnet is enclosed, and it is the structural difference from electrostatics, where enclosing a single charge does give a non-zero flux.

The other three options all assume an isolated pole acts as a source of flux the way a charge does; no such source exists.

questions.q: A current-carrying loop is placed in a uniform magnetic field with its normal at 40° to the field. What does the loop experience?
options: A net force but no torque
Both a net force and a torque
Neither a net force nor a torque
A torque but no net force
questions.concept: Force and torque on a dipole in a uniform field
questions.why:
The forces on opposite sides of the loop are equal in size and opposite in direction, so they cancel and the net force is zero: the loop turns but its centre does not move. They are not in line, however, so they form a couple, giving τ = μB sin 40°, which is not zero. A net force on a dipole requires a non-uniform field, which is why a magnet is pulled towards a nail while a compass needle only swings.

Any option giving a net force ignores the cancellation; 'neither' would require the normal to lie along B.

questions.q: An electron travels in a circle of radius 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m with a period of 1.5 × 10⁻¹⁶ s. Take e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Calculate the magnitude of its orbital magnetic moment.
questions.concept: Orbital magnetic moment of an electron
questions.why:
The circulating electron is a current I = e/T = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹/1.5 × 10⁻¹⁶ = 1.067 × 10⁻³ A round an area A = πr² = π(2.0 × 10⁻¹⁰)² = 1.257 × 10⁻¹⁹ m². So μ = IA = 1.34 × 10⁻²² A·m² (accept 1.3 to 1.4 × 10⁻²²), directed opposite to the angular momentum because the charge is negative.

5.36 × 10⁻²² uses the diameter as the radius; 1.34 × 10⁻¹² uses the circumference 2πr in place of the area πr²; 3.02 × 10⁻⁵⁴ multiplies the charge by the period instead of dividing.

questions.q: A charge of 4.0 μC moves at 3.0 × 10⁵ m/s through a uniform magnetic field of 0.60 T, its velocity making 25° with the field. Calculate the magnitude of the magnetic force on it.
questions.concept: Magnetic force on a moving charge
questions.why:
F = qvB sin θ with θ the angle between v and B: F = (4.0 × 10⁻⁶)(3.0 × 10⁵)(0.60)(sin 25°) = 0.720 × 0.4226 = 0.304 N (accept 0.30 to 0.31 N). The force is perpendicular to both v and B.

0.653 N uses cos 25°, which would make the force greatest when v lies along B and zero when it is perpendicular, the opposite of the truth; 0.720 N assumes v is perpendicular to B and drops the sine; 3.04 × 10⁻⁴ N reads μC as 10⁻⁹ C.

questions.q: An electron (m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) enters a uniform field of 4.0 mT at 5.0 × 10⁶ m/s, perpendicular to the field. Calculate the radius of its circular path.
questions.concept: Radius of a charged particle's circular path
questions.why:
The magnetic force supplies the centripetal force, qvB = mv²/r, so r = mv/(qB) = (9.11 × 10⁻³¹)(5.0 × 10⁶)/[(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)(4.0 × 10⁻³)] = 4.555 × 10⁻²⁴/6.4 × 10⁻²² = 7.1 × 10⁻³ m = 7.1 mm (accept 7.0 to 7.2 mm).

7.1 μm leaves the field as 4.0 T instead of 4.0 mT; 3.6 × 10⁴ m keeps mv² in the numerator and never cancels the extra factor of v; 1.4 × 10² m inverts the formula and computes qB/mv.

questions.q: A proton (m = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves in a circle in a uniform field of 0.60 T. Calculate the frequency of its circular motion.
questions.concept: Cyclotron frequency
questions.why:
T = 2πm/(qB), so f = qB/(2πm) = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)(0.60)/[2π(1.67 × 10⁻²⁷)] = 9.6 × 10⁻²⁰/1.049 × 10⁻²⁶ = 9.15 × 10⁶ Hz = 9.15 MHz (accept 9.0 to 9.3 MHz). The speed does not appear, so the frequency is the same whatever the radius.

57.5 MHz leaves out the 2π; 1.46 MHz divides by 2π a second time; 18.3 MHz uses T = πm/qB, dropping the factor 2 and so doubling f.

questions.q: In a velocity selector a uniform field E = 2.4 × 10⁵ V/m is perpendicular to a uniform field B = 0.30 T. A beam contains protons and doubly charged helium ions with a wide range of speeds. Which particles cross the region undeflected?
options: Any particle in the beam, at 7.2 × 10⁴ m/s
Any particle in the beam, at 8.0 × 10⁵ m/s
Only the helium ions, at 4.0 × 10⁵ m/s
questions.concept: Velocity selector condition
questions.why:
Undeflected means the electric and magnetic forces cancel: qE = qvB, so v = E/B = 2.4 × 10⁵/0.30 = 8.0 × 10⁵ m/s (accept 7.9 to 8.1 × 10⁵). The charge cancels out and the mass never appears, so every particle at that one speed passes, whatever its charge or mass, and every particle at any other speed is deflected.

The two options that pick one species assume q or m survives the cancellation; 7.2 × 10⁴ m/s multiplies E by B instead of dividing.

questions.q: A straight wire 0.35 m long carries 6.0 A and lies at 30° to a uniform field of 0.80 T. Calculate the force on the wire.
questions.concept: Force on a current-carrying wire
questions.why:
F = BIL sin θ with θ between the current and B: F = (0.80)(6.0)(0.35)(sin 30°) = 1.68 × 0.500 = 0.84 N (accept 0.83 to 0.85 N), directed perpendicular to the plane holding the wire and the field.

1.45 N uses cos 30°, which would make a wire laid along the field feel the greatest force instead of none; 1.68 N is the maximum BIL, for a wire at right angles to B; 84 N leaves the length in centimetres.

questions.q: A charged particle is released from rest in a region containing a uniform magnetic field and no electric field. What happens to it?
options: It moves in a circle at constant speed
It accelerates along the field lines
questions.concept: Magnetic force on a stationary charge
questions.why:
The magnetic force is F = qvB sin θ, which is zero when v = 0. With no electric field there is nothing else to push the charge, so it feels no force at all and stays where it is, indefinitely. A magnetic field can bend the path of a charge that is already moving, but it can never start one moving, and it can never change a particle's kinetic energy because the force it exerts is always perpendicular to the velocity.

Circular and helical motion both require the particle to be launched with a speed; acceleration along the field lines is what an electric field would produce.

questions.q: An X-ray has a wavelength of 0.10 nm. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s and c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Calculate the energy of one X-ray photon.
questions.concept: Photon energy from wavelength
questions.why:
In vacuum c = fλ, so f = c/λ = 3.0 × 10⁸/1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 3.0 × 10¹⁸ Hz, and E = hf = hc/λ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴)(3.0 × 10¹⁸) = 1.99 × 10⁻¹⁵ J (accept 1.9 to 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁵). That is about 12 keV, which is why X-rays ionise and radio waves do not.

1.99 × 10⁻²⁴ J leaves the wavelength in nanometres; 6.63 × 10⁻²⁴ J uses h/λ and omits c; 1.99 × 10⁻³⁵ J multiplies by λ instead of dividing by it.

questions.q: A charge of +5.0 μC moves along +x at 2.0 × 10⁵ m/s. A field B = 0.50 T points along +y and a field E = 8.0 × 10⁴ V/m also points along +y. Calculate the magnitude of the total force on the charge.
questions.concept: Adding the electric and magnetic parts of the Lorentz force
questions.why:
F_B = qvB = (5.0 × 10⁻⁶)(2.0 × 10⁵)(0.50) = 0.50 N, and since x̂ × ŷ = ẑ it points along +z. F_E = qE = (5.0 × 10⁻⁶)(8.0 × 10⁴) = 0.40 N along +y. The two are perpendicular, so they add as vectors: F = √(0.50² + 0.40²) = √0.41 = 0.64 N (accept 0.63 to 0.65 N).

0.90 N adds the magnitudes, which is only valid when the two forces are parallel; 0.10 N subtracts them as if they opposed; 0.41 N is the sum of the squares with the square root forgotten.

questions.q: A proton (m = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) enters a uniform field of 0.30 T at 5.0 × 10⁶ m/s, its velocity at 60° to the field. Calculate the pitch of its helical path, the distance it advances along the field per turn.
questions.concept: Pitch of a helical path
questions.why:
The component along B is untouched by the magnetic force: v∥ = v cos 60° = 2.5 × 10⁶ m/s. The period is T = 2πm/(qB) = 2π(1.67 × 10⁻²⁷)/[(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)(0.30)] = 2.19 × 10⁻⁷ s, and it does not contain v. Pitch = v∥T = (2.5 × 10⁶)(2.19 × 10⁻⁷) = 0.547 m (accept 0.53 to 0.56 m).

0.947 m uses v sin 60°, the component that goes round the circle rather than along the axis; 1.09 m uses the full speed; 0.151 m is the radius of the helix, mv⊥/qB, not the pitch.

questions.q: A square coil of 30 turns and side 12 cm sits in a uniform field of 0.45 T with the plane of the coil at 55° to the field. Calculate the flux linkage NΦ of the coil.
questions.concept: Magnetic flux linkage of a coil
questions.why:
A = (0.12)² = 1.44 × 10⁻² m². The angle in Φ = BA cos θ is measured from the normal, and the plane is at 55° to B, so the normal is at 35°. NΦ = (30)(0.45)(1.44 × 10⁻²)(cos 35°) = 0.1944 × 0.8192 = 0.159 Wb (accept 0.157 to 0.161 Wb).

0.112 Wb reads the 55° as the angle from the normal; 0.194 Wb assumes the maximum-flux orientation with the normal along B; 5.31 × 10⁻³ Wb gives the flux through one turn and leaves out the 30 turns.

questions.q: Two coils have self-inductances of 40 mH and 90 mH, and a mutual inductance of 36 mH. Calculate their coupling coefficient.
questions.concept: Coupling coefficient of two coils
questions.why:
M = k√(L₁L₂), so k = M/√(L₁L₂) = 36/√(40 × 90) = 36/√3600 = 36/60 = 0.60 (accept 0.59 to 0.61). It is dimensionless, the millihenries cancel, and it must lie between 0 and 1.

0.90 divides M by L₁ alone; 0.36 squares M as well, using M²/(L₁L₂); 0.28 divides M by the sum L₁ + L₂ instead of by the square root of their product.

questions.q: A coil of 150 turns and area 2.5 × 10⁻³ m² has a total circuit resistance of 6.0 Ω and lies with its normal along a uniform field. The field falls steadily from 0.90 T to 0.30 T. Calculate the charge that circulates.
questions.concept: Charge circulated during a flux change
questions.why:
Integrating I = ε/R over the change gives q = NΔΦ/R, with no time in it. ΔΦ per turn = AΔB = (2.5 × 10⁻³)(0.60) = 1.5 × 10⁻³ Wb, so q = (150)(1.5 × 10⁻³)/6.0 = 0.0375 C (accept 0.037 to 0.038 C). Making the same change ten times more slowly gives the same charge.

0.225 C forgets to divide by the resistance; 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ C leaves out the 150 turns; 0.0563 C uses the starting field 0.90 T instead of the change 0.60 T.

questions.q: A coil of 300 turns and area 0.025 m² rotates at 1800 revolutions per minute in a uniform field of 0.18 T, about an axis perpendicular to the field. Calculate the rms emf it delivers.
questions.concept: Rms emf of an a.c. generator
questions.why:
f = 1800/60 = 30 Hz, so ω = 2πf = 188.5 rad/s. Peak emf ε₀ = NBAω = (300)(0.18)(0.025)(188.5) = 254.5 V, and ε_rms = ε₀/√2 = 180 V (accept 178 to 182 V).

255 V quotes the peak instead of the rms; 28.6 V uses f = 30 in place of ω = 2πf; 1720 V feeds 1800 rev/min straight in as though it were an angular speed in rad/s.

questions.q: An air-cored solenoid has 500 turns wound over a length of 20 cm, with a cross-sectional area of 8.0 cm². Take μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A. Calculate its self-inductance.
questions.concept: Self-inductance of a solenoid
questions.why:
L = μ₀N²A/ℓ = (4π × 10⁻⁷)(500²)(8.0 × 10⁻⁴)/(0.20) = (1.2566 × 10⁻⁶)(2.5 × 10⁵)(8.0 × 10⁻⁴)/0.20 = 1.26 × 10⁻³ H = 1.26 mH (accept 1.24 to 1.28 mH). The current in the coil does not enter: L depends on geometry and core only.

12.6 μH leaves the length in centimetres; 2.51 μH uses N in place of N², missing that doubling the turns both doubles the field and doubles the linkage; 12.6 H leaves the area in cm².

questions.q: A flat coil of 80 turns and area 0.015 m² lies with its plane perpendicular to a uniform field of 0.40 T. The coil is turned right over, through 180°, in 0.25 s. Calculate the average emf induced.
questions.concept: Average emf when a coil is reversed
questions.why:
Flux per turn starts at BA = (0.40)(0.015) = 6.0 × 10⁻³ Wb and ends at −6.0 × 10⁻³ Wb, because cos 180° = −1. The change is therefore 2BA = 1.2 × 10⁻² Wb, not BA. ε = NΔΦ/Δt = (80)(1.2 × 10⁻²)/0.25 = 3.84 V (accept 3.8 to 3.9 V).

1.92 V uses ΔΦ = BA and misses that reversing the coil doubles the change; 0.048 V omits the 80 turns; 7.68 V doubles the change a second time.

questions.q: The current in a 45 mH inductor rises steadily from 0.50 A to 3.5 A in 12 ms. Calculate the magnitude of the self-induced emf during the change.
questions.concept: Back emf from a changing current
questions.why:
ε = L dI/dt. Here dI/dt = (3.5 − 0.50)/0.012 = 250 A/s, so ε = (0.045)(250) = 11.3 V (accept 11.0 to 11.5 V). The emf is set by the rate of change, not by how large the current is.

13.1 V uses the final current 3.5 A instead of the change 3.0 A; 0.135 V multiplies L by ΔI and never divides by the time; 1.13 × 10⁻² V leaves the 12 ms as 12 s.

questions.q: A closed conducting coil is placed in a magnetic field. Which of the following produces no induced emf in it at all?
options: Rotating it steadily about an axis at right angles to the field
Moving it at constant velocity while it stays entirely inside a uniform field
Pulling it out of the field region
Holding it still while the field strength is steadily increased
questions.concept: What changes the flux through a coil
questions.why:
An emf appears only when the flux Φ = BA cos θ through the coil changes. A coil moving inside a uniform field keeps the same B, the same enclosed area and the same orientation, so Φ is constant and the emf is zero however fast it travels. Motion is not the criterion; a changing flux is.

Rotating changes θ, and is how a generator works; pulling the coil out changes the effective area; increasing the field changes B, and needs no motion at all, which is how a transformer works.

questions.q: A long solenoid has 1500 turns per metre and its current rises steadily at 40 A/s. A search coil of 60 turns and area 3.0 cm² is wound round its middle, on the same axis. Take μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A. Calculate the emf induced in the search coil.
questions.concept: Emf induced by a changing solenoid current
questions.why:
Inside the solenoid B = μ₀nI, so dB/dt = μ₀n(dI/dt) = (4π × 10⁻⁷)(1500)(40) = 7.54 × 10⁻² T/s. The search coil links that changing field: ε = NA(dB/dt) = (60)(3.0 × 10⁻⁴)(7.54 × 10⁻²) = 1.36 × 10⁻³ V = 1.36 mV (accept 1.32 to 1.40 mV). Nothing moves anywhere in this arrangement.

22.6 μV omits the search coil's 60 turns; 33.9 mV uses the solenoid's 1500 in place of the search coil's 60; 13.6 V leaves the area in cm².

questions.q: A single circular loop lies with its plane perpendicular to a uniform field of 0.50 T. The loop is squeezed so that its radius shrinks at a steady 3.0 cm/s. Calculate the induced emf at the instant the radius is 20 cm.
questions.concept: Emf from a changing loop area
questions.why:
Here B and θ are fixed and only the area changes, so ε = B dA/dt. With A = πr², dA/dt = 2πr(dr/dt) = 2π(0.20)(0.030) = 3.77 × 10⁻² m²/s. Then ε = (0.50)(3.77 × 10⁻²) = 1.88 × 10⁻² V = 18.8 mV (accept 18.5 to 19.1 mV).

9.4 mV uses πr in place of 2πr; 37.7 mV uses the diameter 0.40 m as the radius; 1.88 V leaves the shrink rate in centimetres per second.

questions.q: A generator coil of 150 turns and area 0.020 m² spins in a uniform field of 0.40 T about an axis perpendicular to the field, and delivers a peak emf of 60 V. Calculate its rotation rate in revolutions per second.
questions.concept: Rotation rate from the peak emf
questions.why:
ε₀ = NBAω, so ω = ε₀/(NBA) = 60/[(150)(0.40)(0.020)] = 60/1.20 = 50.0 rad/s. Then f = ω/2π = 50.0/6.283 = 7.96 rev/s (accept 7.9 to 8.0 rev/s), which is 478 rev/min.

50 rev/s quotes the angular speed in rad/s as a rotation rate; 1.27 rev/s divides by 2π twice; 11.3 rev/s treats the 60 V as an rms value and multiplies it by √2 before dividing.

questions.q: A copper ring is dropped from just above the north pole of a strong vertical bar magnet, so that it falls towards the magnet. While it approaches, how does its downward acceleration compare with g?
options: Equal to g, because the ring carries no current of its own
questions.concept: Lenz's law and the motion that causes it
questions.why:
As the ring approaches, the flux through it grows, so a current is induced. By Lenz's law that current opposes the change, making the ring's lower face a north pole, which the magnet's north pole repels. The ring therefore feels an upward magnetic force on top of its weight, and its acceleration is less than g. The energy for the heat dissipated in the ring comes out of the kinetic energy it fails to gain.

An acceleration equal to g ignores the induced current; greater than g would mean the induced current speeds up the very change that creates it, which would manufacture energy from nothing; zero would need the two forces to balance exactly, which is not required here.

questions.q: A coil of 200 turns and area 8.0 × 10⁻³ m² has a total resistance of 5.0 Ω. Its normal lies along a uniform field whose strength changes at a steady 1.5 T/s. Calculate the power dissipated in the coil.
questions.concept: Power dissipated by an induced current
questions.why:
ε = NA(dB/dt) = (200)(8.0 × 10⁻³)(1.5) = 2.40 V, so I = ε/R = 2.40/5.0 = 0.48 A and P = I²R = (0.48)²(5.0) = 1.15 W (accept 1.13 to 1.17 W). Checking with ε²/R = 5.76/5.0 gives the same 1.15 W.

5.76 W is ε² with the division by R forgotten; 28.8 W multiplies by R instead of dividing, using ε²R; 2.9 × 10⁻⁵ W leaves out the 200 turns.

questions.q: An aircraft of wingspan 32 m flies horizontally at 250 m/s where the vertical component of the Earth's magnetic field is 4.5 × 10⁻⁵ T. Calculate the emf induced between its wingtips.
questions.concept: Motional emf across a moving conductor
questions.why:
The wings act as a conductor of length L moving at right angles both to their own length and to the vertical field component, so ε = BLv = (4.5 × 10⁻⁵)(32)(250) = 0.36 V (accept 0.35 to 0.37 V). The wingtips are not joined by a circuit, so there is an emf but no current and no retarding force.

1.44 × 10⁻³ V multiplies B by L and leaves out the speed; 8.0 × 10³ V multiplies L by v and leaves out the field; 3.6 V is a power-of-ten slip in the field.

questions.q: A rod of length 0.50 m slides at a steady 3.0 m/s on frictionless rails in a field of 0.40 T perpendicular to the plane of the circuit. The total resistance is 0.25 Ω. Calculate the applied force needed and the mechanical power supplied.
questions.concept: Retarding force and mechanical power on a sliding rod
questions.why:
ε = BLv = (0.40)(0.50)(3.0) = 0.60 V, so I = ε/R = 0.60/0.25 = 2.4 A. The current in the field gives a retarding force F = BIL = (0.40)(2.4)(0.50) = 0.48 N, which the applied force must match for steady speed. Then P = Fv = (0.48)(3.0) = 1.44 W (accept 1.42 to 1.46 W), and the check I²R = (2.4)²(0.25) = 1.44 W agrees exactly.

0.12 N and 0.36 W use the emf in place of the current, forgetting to divide by R; 0.96 N and 2.88 W use B²Lv/R with only one factor of L; 0.48 N and 0.48 W quote the force as the power and leave out the speed.

questions.q: A conducting loop lies flat in the plane of the page. A uniform magnetic field points out of the page through the loop and is being steadily switched off. As seen by the reader, which way does the induced current flow, and which way does its own field point inside the loop?
options: Clockwise, with its own field into the page
Clockwise, with its own field out of the page
Anticlockwise, with its own field out of the page
Anticlockwise, with its own field into the page
questions.concept: Direction of an induced current
questions.why:
Lenz's law opposes the change, not the field. The outward flux is shrinking, so the induced current must act to maintain it, setting up a field inside the loop that also points out of the page. By the right-hand grip rule, a field out of the page needs an anticlockwise current as seen by the reader.

The two 'into the page' options oppose the field itself rather than its loss, which is the answer for a field that is growing; the clockwise-and-out-of-the-page option pairs the correct field with the wrong circulation sense.

questions.q: An appliance rated at 2.0 kW, 110 V is to be run from a 330 V line through an ideal transformer. What is the turns ratio N₂/N₁, and what type of transformer is it?
questions.concept: Turns ratio for a step-up or step-down transformer
questions.why:
The primary is always the side fed by the source, so V₁ = 330 V, and the appliance is the load on the secondary, so V₂ = 110 V. Then N₂/N₁ = V₂/V₁ = 110/330 = 1/3. Since N₂ is less than N₁ this is a step-down transformer.

The options giving 3 take the appliance as the primary and invert the ratio; calling a ratio of 1/3 step-up misreads the definition, which is fixed by N₂ against N₁, not by which number looks bigger. The 2.0 kW rating is not needed for this part.

questions.q: A 1500 W appliance rated for 100 V is run from a 250 V outlet through an ideal transformer. What current does it draw from the outlet?
questions.concept: Primary and secondary currents in a transformer
questions.why:
The outlet feeds the primary, so the current drawn from it is I₁ = P/V₁ = 1500/250 = 6.0 A (accept 5.9 to 6.1 A). Check with power in equals power out: the appliance itself carries I₂ = 1500/100 = 15 A, and I₁V₁ = 6.0 × 250 = 1500 W = 15 × 100 ✓.

15 A is the current in the appliance, not the one drawn from the outlet; 2.4 A multiplies the answer by the turns ratio a second time; 37.5 A uses I₁/I₂ = N₂/N₁ upside down, so the voltage and the current are both stepped the same way.

questions.q: An ideal transformer has a turns ratio N₂/N₁ = 5 and a 300 Ω resistor connected across its secondary. What resistance does the source connected to the primary see?
questions.concept: Resistance seen through a transformer
questions.why:
The load seen from the primary is V₁/I₁ = R/(N₂/N₁)² = 300/5² = 300/25 = 12 Ω (accept 11.8 to 12.2 Ω). The turns ratio enters squared, because the voltage is divided by 5 while the current is multiplied by 5.

60 Ω divides by the ratio instead of by its square; 1500 Ω and 7500 Ω multiply rather than divide, which would make a step-up transformer present a larger load than the resistor itself.

questions.q: A signal source that delivers maximum power into 800 Ω is to drive an 8.0 Ω load through an ideal matching transformer. What turns ratio N₂/N₁ is required?
questions.concept: Impedance matching with a transformer
questions.why:
Matching means the primary must see 800 Ω when 8.0 Ω is on the secondary: 800 = 8.0/(N₂/N₁)², so (N₂/N₁)² = 8.0/800 = 0.010 and N₂/N₁ = √0.010 = 1/10. The secondary has one tenth as many turns, a step-down transformer.

1/100 stops at the resistance ratio and forgets the square root; 10 and 100 invert the ratio, which would make the source see 80 kΩ instead of 800 Ω.

questions.q: In a transformer the flux in the core is changing at 0.045 Wb/s at a certain instant. The primary has 800 turns and the secondary has 200 turns. Calculate the emf induced in the secondary at that instant.
questions.concept: Induced emf from the rate of change of core flux
questions.why:
The same flux threads both windings, and Faraday's law applied to the secondary gives ε₂ = N₂ dΦ/dt = (200)(0.045) = 9.0 V (accept 8.9 to 9.1 V). Applied to the primary it gives 36 V, and the ratio 9.0/36 = 200/800 as expected.

36 V uses the primary turns; 45 V uses the total 1000 turns of both windings, but each coil links the flux separately; 0.045 V leaves out the turns count altogether.

questions.q: A generator delivers 30 kW at 400 V. An ideal transformer steps this up to 12 kV before it is sent along a transmission line of total resistance 8.0 Ω. Calculate the power lost as heat in the line.
questions.concept: Power loss in a transmission line
questions.why:
The line carries I = P/V = 30 000/12 000 = 2.5 A, so the loss is I²R = (2.5)²(8.0) = 50 W (accept 49 to 51 W), about 0.17 per cent of what is sent.

45 kW is what the same line would lose at 400 V, where the current is 75 A, more than the power being transmitted, which is the whole reason for stepping up; 20 W forgets to square the current; 2.0 × 10⁴ W uses V²/R with the supply voltage, but the 400 V is not the voltage dropped across the line.

questions.q: A transformer core is built from thin sheets of metal insulated from one another rather than from one solid block. What does this construction reduce?
options: The heating caused by eddy currents in the core
The I²R heating in the copper windings
The frequency of the secondary output
The current drawn by the load
questions.concept: Why a transformer core is laminated
questions.why:
The changing flux induces currents in the conducting core itself, just as it does in the windings. Those eddy currents circulate in loops and waste energy as heat. Insulating thin laminations from each other breaks up the paths those loops would take, so far less current can circulate, while the useful flux through the core is unaffected.

Winding losses depend on the resistance of the copper and are unchanged by the core; the frequency is the same on both sides whatever the core is made of; the load current is fixed by the load and the secondary voltage.

questions.q: A transformer designed for a 50 Hz a.c. supply is connected by mistake to a 12 V battery. Once any switch-on transient has died away, what voltage appears across the secondary terminals?
options: 12 V, the same as the primary
12 V multiplied by the turns ratio
A voltage that rises steadily with time
questions.concept: Why a transformer needs alternating current
questions.why:
A transformer works through Faraday's law, ε = −N dΦ/dt. A battery drives a steady current, so once the transient is over the core flux is constant, dΦ/dt = 0, and the secondary emf is exactly zero. Meanwhile the primary has no back emf to limit it and draws a current set only by its own small winding resistance, so it is likely to overheat.

The two options giving a voltage assume the turns ratio acts on any voltage at all, but the ratio only follows from a shared changing flux; a steadily rising output would require a flux that accelerates without limit.
